The idea says a coin's large fall yesterday predicts a bounce, so the factor should be high for coins with a large negative return over the past day. The simplest form is minus the one-day return. I'll start there.

The idea is about the close sitting far above the open, so the plainest first form is the log of the ratio close/open — a unit-free, comparable measure of how far price moved up from the low. I'll start with that.

The incremental IC is exactly 0.0000, meaning the raw close-over-open gap is entirely absorbed by the short-term reversal style — it's mostly yesterday's move. So the plain ratio carries no independent information. I'll keep the direction but measure the same thing over a longer stretch: the average position above the open over the last 5 days, which still captures "closing far above its open" but is less dominated by the latest bar.

The longer 5-day average is also at 0.0001 — the size of the gap matters only in its short-term shape, and both forms are entirely reversal. Since the reversal style is removed, I'll measure the same thing in a way that keeps the recent bar but weights it less: the rank of the close above the open within its own recent history, which is a bounded, spike-resistant version of "far above its open".

Three forms of the same quantity — the raw log ratio, the 5-day average of it, and its own 10-day rank — all land at 0.0001 or 0.0002 incremental IC with t-values well below 1, and every period is essentially zero. That says the close-above-open gap carries no information beyond the short-term reversal that is already removed, so on this history coins closing far above their open do not keep rising. I'll stop here rather than spend the last test on a re-encoding of the same data, and hand in the plain version with the direction the idea states.

The idea is about dollar volume relative to other coins, so I'll start with the plainest version: the log of average daily dollar volume over the past month, negated because low volume is expected to be bullish.

incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0011 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0020, 2024 -0.0004

The plain 20-day mean of log dollar volume has almost no incremental content (0.0011, t = 1.9), which suggests the level is mostly a liquidity proxy that is already removed. Since the idea is about coins being *unusually* quiet, I'll measure each coin's dollar volume against its own history over a longer baseline (60 days against 20 days), keeping the negative sign.

The relative-to-own-history version is also essentially flat (−0.0010), so it is not picking up an unusual-activity signal. Since a few extreme quiet coins can dominate a mean, I'll replace the mean with the median of log dollar volume over the same 20-day window.

So on this history the dollar-volume level carries almost no information beyond the liquidity style that is already removed; the relative-to-own-history versions are also flat, which means there is no residual "quiet coin" effect here. I'll stop at the fourth test and hand in the simplest, most faithful form, keeping its negative direction because the idea says low volume is bullish.

The idea is about the daily high-low range, which is a range measured as high/low — a ratio, so it is comparable across coins regardless of price unit. The plainest first form is the log of that ratio averaged over a few days, with the negative sign because wide range is bearish.

What I found: the plain one-day return is entirely the short-term reversal style and has zero incremental IC, but measuring yesterday's fall as the distance from the low up to close keeps a genuine positive signal after the reversal is removed (+0.0127, t = 5.5), and it is positive in all three periods (+0.0166 in 2022H2, +0.0113 in 2023, +0.0122 in 2024), so it isn't a single-period artifact. The bounded shape of the measurement was what mattered, not a longer or noisier window.

That keeps it comparable across coins (no coin-specific price or volume units) and points the way the idea says — low position = bullish.

What I found: measured as a position inside its own recent range of dollar volume, coins with low volume did *worse* over the next days, not better — the rank IC is negative and the incremental IC stays negative after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed. The signal is stable across periods rather than a single-period artifact, so the direction the idea asks for is not supported by this data. I keep the direction as the idea states and hand in the simplest, most faithful form: today's dollar volume ranked inside its own 20-day range.
